note: Source-check dates preserve the checks recorded when these entries were maintained; they are not new replication checks. Source format and claim status are separate. Reported means the cited source reports the result or event, not that independent groups have confirmed it. Preliminary, disputed, and retracted flag the cautions recorded in each summary. Consult the source for methods, publication history, and subsequent updates.

items.title: Fields Medals 2026: Deng, Pardon, Tsimerman, Wang
items.authors: International Mathematical Union
items.summary: At the opening of the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia, the IMU awarded Fields Medals to Yu Deng (rigorously deriving the Boltzmann equation, which describes gases, from the motion of individual colliding particles), John Pardon (symplectic geometry, the mathematics underlying classical mechanics), Jacob Tsimerman (using 'o-minimality', a tool from logic, to prove central conjectures in number theory and geometry) and Hong Wang (harmonic analysis and geometric measure theory, including her work on the Kakeya conjecture). Wang is the third woman to win the medal in its 90-year history.
items.headline: The 2026 Fields Medals recognize four mathematicians

items.title: An OpenAI model has disproved a central conjecture in discrete geometry (the Erdős unit-distance conjecture)
items.authors: OpenAI (reasoning model); commentary by W. T. Gowers and others; preprint write-up "An explicit lower bound for the unit distance problem"
items.venue: OpenAI announcement (20 May 2026); arXiv preprint; Quanta Magazine feature (3 Aug 2026)
items.summary: In 1946 Paul Erdős asked how many pairs among n points in the plane can be exactly one unit apart, and conjectured that arrangements based on square grids are essentially the best possible. In May 2026 OpenAI reported that a general-purpose reasoning model had constructed families of point sets with more unit-distance pairs than the conjectured ceiling, disproving the conjecture after 80 years, using tools from algebraic number theory (class field towers) far from the problem's usual methods. Fields medalist Timothy Gowers called it "a milestone in AI mathematics." Caveats: the result is a lower-bound construction that can be checked directly, which plays to what these systems do well; the true growth rate of the unit-distance count remains open; the write-up is a preprint and the wider mathematical community was still digesting it in September 2026.
items.headline: A reported AI counterexample challenges the unit-distance conjecture

items.title: Abel Prize 2026 awarded to Gerd Faltings
items.authors: Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters
items.summary: Gerd Faltings (Max Planck Institute for Mathematics, Bonn) received the 2026 Abel Prize 'for introducing powerful tools in arithmetic geometry and resolving long-standing diophantine conjectures of Mordell and Lang'. Diophantine problems ask for whole-number or fraction solutions to polynomial equations. In 1983 Faltings proved the Mordell conjecture, open for 60 years: a curve of 'genus' at least 2 (roughly, a surface with two or more holes when viewed over the complex numbers) has only finitely many rational-number points. He is the first German laureate.
items.headline: The 2026 Abel Prize honors Gerd Faltings

items.title: AI and the Erdős problems: from a literature-search embarrassment to the first autonomous solution (Erdős Problem #728)
items.authors: Nat Sothanaphan (writeup); proof by GPT-5.2 Pro with Harmonic's Aristotle in Lean; database by Thomas Bloom; verification by Terence Tao and others
items.venue: arXiv preprint; erdosproblems.com; GitHub wiki 'AI contributions to Erdős problems'
items.summary: Paul Erdős left over a thousand unsolved problems, catalogued since 2024 at Thomas Bloom's erdosproblems.com. In October 2025 OpenAI staff claimed GPT-5 had 'solved' ten of them; Bloom pointed out the model had merely found existing solutions in old papers the database had missed, the posts were deleted, and DeepMind's CEO called the episode embarrassing. Genuine progress followed: in January 2026 a proof of Problem #728 (about when a product of two factorials divides another) was generated by GPT-5.2 Pro, formalised in Lean by the Aristotle system and accepted by Terence Tao as the first Erdős problem fully resolved by AI without human mathematical input. A community wiki now tracks dozens of AI contributions, carefully separating new proofs from literature rediscoveries; a Google study found that of 13 'open' problems its Gemini pipeline attacked, 8 turned out to be already solved in the literature, suggesting many 'open' problems were obscure rather than hard. Bloom warns that many AI-generated proofs are never read by a human. The picture then changed quickly: by mid-2026 several dozen Erdős problems had been resolved with AI assistance, including the unit-distance conjecture (see the separate entry), and Tao's assessment moved from "lowest-hanging fruit" to problems a strong graduate student might solve. Human readers have still found fixable gaps in some AI proofs.
items.headline: AI's work on Erdős problems moves from finding old solutions to new claims

items.title: The Equational Theories Project: Advancing Collaborative Mathematical Research at Scale
items.authors: Matthew Bolan, Joachim Breitner, Jose Brox, Nicholas Carlini, Mario Carneiro, Terence Tao, et al. (34 authors)
items.summary: Launched by Terence Tao in September 2024, this project took the 4,694 simplest equational laws for 'magmas' (sets with one binary operation and no other rules) and decided, for every ordered pair, whether one law implies the other: 22,028,942 implications in all. Every answer was checked in the Lean proof assistant. Most cases were settled by classical automated theorem provers and computer searches, with humans handling the hardest few; the informal work took about two months and the formal verification another five. Several new magma constructions were found, and one implication for finite magmas remains open. Tao notes modern large language models played only a minor role; the paper's point is a model for large-scale, machine-verified collaboration among strangers.
items.headline: A collaborative project maps which algebraic equations imply others

items.title: Advanced version of Gemini with Deep Think officially achieves gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad
items.authors: Google DeepMind (Gemini Deep Think team); separately, OpenAI (experimental reasoning model)
items.venue: Google DeepMind official announcement, graded and certified by IMO coordinators; OpenAI announcement graded by former IMO medallists
items.summary: At the 2025 IMO an advanced version of Google's Gemini model solved 5 of 6 problems perfectly for 35 of 42 points, a gold-medal score, and did so entirely in ordinary English within the 4.5-hour time limit; the IMO's president confirmed the grading. Unlike 2024, no human translated the problems into a formal language and no computer checked the proofs, so the result shows a general language model can write rigorous competition-level proofs. OpenAI announced the same 35/42 score for an unreleased experimental model on the same problems, but its proofs were graded by three former IMO medallists it selected rather than by the IMO, and the announcement drew criticism for its timing. Neither system was an official contestant; five human students scored a perfect 42.
items.headline: Gemini reaches gold-medal standard on an international mathematics contest

items.title: AlphaEvolve: A Gemini-powered coding agent for designing advanced algorithms
items.authors: Alexander Novikov, Ngan Vu, Marvin Eisenberger, et al. (Google DeepMind, 18 authors)
items.venue: Google DeepMind official announcement (14 May 2025); arXiv preprint (16 Jun 2025)
items.summary: AlphaEvolve is an evolutionary system in which Gemini models repeatedly rewrite candidate programs and an automatic evaluator scores them. Its headline result is a way to multiply two 4x4 matrices of complex numbers using 48 scalar multiplications, beating the 49 from Strassen's 1969 method that had stood for 56 years in this setting (fewer multiplications means faster algorithms for large matrices). Tested on more than 50 open mathematical problems it matched the best known answer about 75% of the time and improved it in about 20%, including a new lower bound of 593 for the 'kissing number' in 11 dimensions (how many equal spheres can touch a central one). The improvements are small and numerical rather than conceptual, but they are machine-verifiable, and the same system has reportedly recovered 0.7% of Google's global compute through better scheduling.
items.headline: An AI coding agent searches for improved algorithms

items.title: Maximum Flow and Minimum-Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time
items.authors: Li Chen, Rasmus Kyng, Yang P. Liu, Richard Peng, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg, Sushant Sachdeva
items.venue: Journal of the ACM, vol. 72, no. 3 (2025); earlier version in FOCS 2022 (Best Paper)
items.summary: The maximum-flow problem asks how much material can be pushed from a source to a sink through a network of pipes with capacities; minimum-cost flow adds a price per unit on each pipe. These problems model everything from traffic and shipping to image segmentation and matching, and had been studied since the 1950s with steadily improving but still super-linear algorithms. This paper gives an algorithm running in m^(1+o(1)) time on a network with m edges, essentially proportional to the time it takes just to read the input, which is as fast as one could hope. The key idea is to solve the problem via a sequence of "minimum-ratio cycle" updates maintained by a new dynamic data structure. First presented at FOCS 2022, where it won the Best Paper award, and published in the Journal of the ACM in 2025.
items.headline: Network-flow algorithms approach the time needed to read their input

items.title: Breaking the Sorting Barrier for Directed Single-Source Shortest Paths
items.authors: Ran Duan, Jiayi Mao, Xiao Mao, Xinkai Shu, Longhui Yin
items.venue: 57th ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 2025), Best Paper Award
items.summary: Finding the shortest route from one point to every other point in a network is one of the oldest problems in computer science, and Dijkstra's 1956 algorithm, which processes vertices in order of distance, was long assumed to be essentially the best possible: its running time on sparse networks is dominated by the cost of sorting the vertices. This paper gives a deterministic algorithm running in about m times (log n) to the power 2/3, beating Dijkstra's m plus n log n on sparse graphs, by cleverly avoiding a full sort of the frontier. It won a best-paper award at STOC 2025 and complements a 2024 result (Haeupler, Hladík, Rozhoň, Tarjan, Tětek, FOCS 2024) showing Dijkstra is optimal among algorithms that do output the sorted order. The practical speed-up is modest; the significance is that a textbook 'barrier' turned out not to be fundamental.
items.headline: A shortest-path algorithm avoids a long-standing sorting bottleneck

items.title: Abel Prize 2025 awarded to Masaki Kashiwara
items.authors: Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters
items.summary: Masaki Kashiwara of Kyoto University became the first Japanese mathematician to win the Abel Prize, cited for 'fundamental contributions to algebraic analysis and representation theory'. As a 23-year-old master's student he founded the theory of D-modules, which treats systems of differential equations as algebraic objects so they can be studied with tools from algebra and geometry. He later discovered 'crystal bases', combinatorial skeletons of the symmetries that appear in quantum groups, which now underpin much of modern representation theory.
items.headline: The 2025 Abel Prize honors Masaki Kashiwara

items.title: Hilbert's sixth problem: derivation of fluid equations via Boltzmann's kinetic theory
items.authors: Yu Deng, Zaher Hani, Xiao Ma
items.summary: In 1900 David Hilbert asked mathematicians to put physics on rigorous footing, including deriving the equations of fluid flow from the motion of individual particles. Deng, Hani and Ma start from hard spheres bouncing elastically under Newton's laws, show that in the limit of many tiny particles their statistics obey Boltzmann's kinetic equation, and then show that Boltzmann's equation in turn yields the compressible Euler and incompressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations of fluid mechanics. The work builds on Deng's earlier derivation of the Boltzmann equation, cited in his 2026 Fields Medal, and has attracted both acclaim and some critical commentary.
items.headline: A proof connects particle dynamics with equations for fluid motion

items.title: Volume estimates for unions of convex sets, and the Kakeya set conjecture in three dimensions
items.authors: Hong Wang, Joshua Zahl
items.summary: A Kakeya set is a region containing a unit-length needle pointing in every possible direction. Such sets can have zero volume, but the Kakeya conjecture says they cannot be 'thin' in a subtler sense: their fractal (Hausdorff) dimension must equal the dimension of the space. Wang and Zahl proved this in three dimensions in a 127-page paper, resolving a problem open since the 1970s. The conjecture is a linchpin connecting to major open questions in harmonic analysis, and the work contributed to Wang's 2026 Fields Medal.
items.headline: A proof addresses the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture

items.title: 2024 NAEP Mathematics Assessment: Results at Grades 4 and 8 for the Nation, States, and Districts
items.authors: National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), U.S. Department of Education; National Assessment Governing Board
items.venue: The Nation's Report Card (National Assessment of Educational Progress)
items.summary: NAEP is the standardized test the U.S. government gives to a national sample of students every two years, so it is the country's main yardstick for tracking achievement over time. The 2024 mathematics results, released 29 January 2025, showed grade 4 scores up 2 points from 2022 but still 3 points below 2019, with 39% of fourth-graders at or above the Proficient level; grade 8 scores were flat versus 2022 and 8 points below 2019. The recovery was concentrated among higher-performing students, while the lowest performers did not improve, widening the gap between the top and bottom of the distribution.
items.headline: US mathematics assessments track student performance and persistent gaps

items.title: FrontierMath: A Benchmark for Evaluating Advanced Mathematical Reasoning in AI
items.authors: Elliot Glazer, Ege Erdil, Tamay Besiroglu, Diego Chicharro, Evan Chen, et al. (Epoch AI, 24 authors)
items.venue: arXiv preprint; Epoch AI benchmark hub
items.summary: FrontierMath is a private set of hundreds of original research-level maths problems written and vetted by professional mathematicians, each with an automatically checkable answer, designed so models cannot have memorised them from the internet. At launch in November 2024 every leading AI model solved under 2%, versus near-saturation on older school-level benchmarks. Scores then rose fast: by early 2026 top models were still below 10% on the hardest 'Tier 4' set, and by August 2026 Epoch's leaderboard reported 83% on Tier 4 for the best model. Caveats: in June 2026 Epoch issued a corrected 'v2' after finding errors in over 100 problems; OpenAI funded the benchmark and had access to much of it; and a benchmark measures answers to set problems, not the ability to do open-ended research.
items.headline: A benchmark tests AI on difficult mathematical problems

items.title: GIMPS discovers largest known prime number: 2^136279841 - 1
items.authors: Luke Durant; Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search (GIMPS)
items.summary: A Mersenne prime is a prime number of the form 2^p - 1. On 12 October 2024 the Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search confirmed that 2^136,279,841 - 1, a number with 41,024,320 digits, is prime, making it the 52nd known Mersenne prime and the largest known prime of any kind. Discoverer Luke Durant, a former NVIDIA engineer, ran the search across thousands of data-centre GPUs in 17 countries, ending a 28-year streak of such records being set on ordinary personal computers.
items.headline: A distributed search finds a new largest known prime

items.title: AI achieves silver-medal standard solving International Mathematical Olympiad problems (AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2)
items.authors: Google DeepMind (AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry teams; Nature paper by T. Hubert, R. Mehta, L. Sartran et al.)
items.venue: Google DeepMind official announcement (25 Jul 2024); Nature (12 Nov 2025)
items.summary: Two DeepMind systems together solved 4 of the 6 problems from the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad (the world's top high-school maths competition), scoring 28 of 42 points, a silver-medal level, with the solutions graded by Fields medallist Timothy Gowers and IMO medallist Joseph Myers. AlphaProof learned by reinforcement learning to write proofs in Lean, a 'proof assistant' language in which every step is checked by computer, so its answers cannot be wrong; AlphaGeometry 2 handled the geometry problem in 19 seconds. Caveats: humans first translated the problems into Lean, and some solutions took days rather than the contestants' 4.5 hours. The AlphaProof method was later peer-reviewed and published in Nature in November 2025.
items.headline: AI systems reach silver-medal standard on Olympiad problems

items.title: Determination of the fifth Busy Beaver value (BB(5) = 47,176,870, verified in Coq)
items.authors: The bbchallenge Collaboration (Justin Blanchard, Daniel Briggs, Konrad Deka, Nathan Fenner, Yannick Forster, mxdys, et al.)
items.venue: bbchallenge official announcement (2 Jul 2024); arXiv preprint (15 Sep 2025)
items.summary: The Busy Beaver function BB(n) is the longest any n-state Turing machine (the simplest mathematical model of a computer) can run before halting; it grows faster than any computable function, so each value is a landmark. Around 1989-1990 Marxen and Buntrock found a 5-state machine that runs 47,176,870 steps, and an online collaboration of hobbyists and researchers spent two years proving no 5-state machine runs longer, by classifying roughly 180 million machines with automated 'deciders'. Crucially the whole proof was written in the Coq (now Rocq) proof assistant, so a computer checked every case; it compiles in about 10 hours on a laptop. It is the first new Busy Beaver value in over 40 years and the first ever formally verified. BB(6) is known to be astronomically large and is probably out of reach.
items.headline: A machine-checked proof settles the five-state Busy Beaver value

items.title: Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture I: construction of the functor
items.authors: Dennis Gaitsgory, Sam Raskin (series with D. Arinkin, D. Beraldo, J. Campbell, L. Chen, J. Faergeman, K. Lin, N. Rozenblyum)
items.summary: The Langlands program is a web of conjectures connecting number theory (equations and their symmetries) to analysis (a family of highly symmetric functions), sometimes called a 'grand unified theory of mathematics'. The geometric version replaces number systems with curves over a field, where the conjecture predicts that two very different mathematical categories are secretly the same. In May 2024 a nine-person team led by Gaitsgory and Raskin posted five papers totalling roughly 1,000 pages that prove the geometric Langlands conjecture in the de Rham setting, the culmination of about 30 years of work.
items.headline: A major proof connects geometry with representations of symmetry

items.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
items.authors: Ziming Liu, Yixuan Wang, Sachin Vaidya, Fabian Ruehle, James Halverson, Marin Soljacic, Thomas Y. Hou, Max Tegmark
items.venue: arXiv preprint; accepted to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2025
items.summary: Standard neural networks (multi-layer perceptrons) combine inputs with learned weights and then apply a fixed nonlinear function at each node. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks flip this: the learnable parts are the functions themselves, represented as flexible curves (splines) on the connections, inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, which says any continuous function of several variables can be built from sums of one-variable functions. The authors report that small KANs match or beat much larger conventional networks on curve-fitting and differential-equation tasks and are easier to interpret, even rediscovering symbolic formulas. Although accepted to ICLR 2025, the claims about scaling and speed remain actively debated and independent evaluations have been mixed, so treat this as a promising early idea rather than settled.
items.headline: A neural-network design learns functions along its connections

items.title: Abel Prize 2024 awarded to Michel Talagrand
items.authors: Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters
items.summary: The Abel Prize is an annual award for lifetime achievement in mathematics, given by the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters. Michel Talagrand (CNRS, Paris) received it for his work on randomness: sharp estimates for the largest value a random process is likely to reach, 'concentration of measure' (the surprising fact that a quantity depending on many independent random inputs is usually very close to its average), and a rigorous proof of physicist Giorgio Parisi's formula for spin glasses, a type of disordered magnetic material.
items.headline: The 2024 Abel Prize honors Michel Talagrand

items.title: Solving olympiad geometry without human demonstrations (AlphaGeometry)
items.authors: Trieu H. Trinh, Yuhuai Wu, Quoc V. Le, He He, Thang Luong
items.summary: AlphaGeometry solved 25 of 30 past IMO geometry problems under competition time limits, close to the 25.9 average of human gold medallists and far above the previous best automated system's 10. It is 'neuro-symbolic': a language model suggests which auxiliary points or lines to add to a diagram, and a rule-based deduction engine then grinds out the consequences, so every proof it produces is machine-checkable. Because almost no human-written geometry proofs exist in a machine-readable form, the team trained the model on 100 million synthetic theorems and proofs it generated itself. The code and model were released publicly.
items.headline: AlphaGeometry solves contest geometry problems using learned guidance and deduction

explainer.finding: AlphaGeometry solved 25 of 30 selected olympiad geometry problems, combining learned suggestions with symbolic deduction.
explainer.method: A model trained on synthetic examples proposed helpful geometric constructions, while a deduction engine pursued proofs. The authors evaluated it on a defined problem set.
explainer.meaning: Adding an auxiliary line can turn a difficult diagram into familiar relationships. The learned system suggests such moves; the symbolic system checks their consequences.
explainer.limits: Success on this geometry benchmark does not establish general mathematical reasoning or mastery of every kind of proof. The formal representation limits the problems addressed.

items.title: Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models (FunSearch)
items.authors: Bernardino Romera-Paredes, Mohammadamin Barekatain, Alexander Novikov, Matej Balog, M. Pawan Kumar, Emilien Dupont, Francisco J. R. Ruiz, Jordan S. Ellenberg, Pengming Wang, Omar Fawzi, Pushmeet Kohli, Alhussein Fawzi
items.summary: FunSearch pairs a language model that writes short computer programs with an automatic checker that scores them, keeping and mutating the best. Applied to the 'cap set' problem, which asks for the largest set of points in a high-dimensional grid with no three in a line, it found constructions larger than any previously known, including a new record in dimension 8, described by DeepMind as the biggest advance on the problem in 20 years. It also produced better-than-standard heuristics for bin packing (fitting items into as few containers as possible). The point is not that the model 'understood' the maths, but that searching over verifiable programs let it find genuinely new objects; the outputs are readable code a mathematician can inspect.
items.headline: Language-model-guided program search produces mathematical discoveries

items.title: Formalization of the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa (Marton) conjecture proof in Lean 4
items.authors: Terence Tao (project lead) with Yael Dillies, Bhavik Mehta and other contributors; original proof by W. T. Gowers, Ben Green, Freddie Manners, Terence Tao
items.venue: GitHub project (teorth/pfr) with Blueprint; original paper 'On a conjecture of Marton', arXiv
items.summary: In November 2023 Gowers, Green, Manners and Tao proved Marton's conjecture, also called the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture: roughly, if a set of binary vectors has few distinct pairwise sums then it must be almost entirely contained in a small number of copies of a structured subspace. Within about three weeks Tao led an open online effort that rewrote the entire proof in the Lean proof assistant, using a 'Blueprint' that links each human-readable step to its formal counterpart, so the computer certified the whole argument. This was the first time a brand-new research result was fully formalised almost as soon as it appeared, and it became the template for later crowdsourced formalisation projects. Later work refined the bound in the theorem (exponent 12 to 9) and formalised that too.
items.headline: A proof assistant checks a major result about additive structure

items.title: PISA 2022 Results (Volume I): The State of Learning and Equity in Education
items.authors: OECD
items.summary: PISA is the OECD's test of 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics and science, run every three years; in 2022 about 690,000 students in 81 countries and economies took it. Average mathematics performance across OECD countries fell by almost 15 score points compared with 2018, an unprecedented drop roughly three times larger than any previous change between consecutive rounds and equivalent to about three-quarters of a year of learning. The report attributes only part of the decline to pandemic disruption, since reading and science had already been slipping for a decade, and notes that about one in four 15-year-olds is now a low performer in mathematics.
items.headline: PISA results compare mathematics learning across education systems

items.title: On a conjecture of Marton
items.authors: W. T. Gowers, Ben Green, Freddie Manners, Terence Tao
items.summary: Marton's conjecture, also called the polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa conjecture, was the central open problem of additive combinatorics. It says that if a set of binary vectors has 'small doubling' (adding any two elements of the set rarely produces something new), then the set is almost a subspace, with only a polynomial amount of loss instead of an exponential one. Gowers, Green, Manners and Tao proved it in characteristic 2 using an entropy-based argument. The proof was then fully formalised in the Lean proof assistant by an online team in about three weeks, a landmark for computer-verified frontier mathematics.
items.headline: A proof links approximate addition patterns to structured sets

items.title: A proof of the Kahn-Kalai conjecture
items.authors: Jinyoung Park, Huy Tuan Pham
items.venue: Journal of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 37, no. 1, pp. 235-243 (published online 2023-08-07)
items.summary: In a random graph you include each possible edge with probability p; the "threshold" is the value of p at which some property (such as containing a Hamiltonian cycle) suddenly switches from very unlikely to very likely. Kahn and Kalai conjectured in 2006 that this true threshold is never more than a logarithmic factor above a much easier-to-compute quantity called the expectation threshold. Park and Pham proved the conjecture in a strikingly short six-page argument, settling a central problem in probabilistic combinatorics and providing a general tool for locating thresholds in many random structures. The work won them the 2024 Dénes König Prize.
items.headline: A proof settles a conjecture about when random structures acquire properties

items.title: New Bounds for Matrix Multiplication: from Alpha to Omega
items.authors: Virginia Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu, Renfei Zhou
items.venue: ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA 2024); arXiv
items.summary: Multiplying two n-by-n matrices the schoolbook way takes about n-cubed operations; the 'exponent of matrix multiplication' omega is the smallest power such that it can be done in roughly n-to-the-omega steps, and it is believed but unproven that omega equals 2. This paper improved the 'laser method' and lowered the best known bound from 2.371866 to 2.371552. In 2024 Alman, Duan, Williams, Xu, Xu and Zhou pushed it further to 2.371339 by adding more asymmetry to the analysis (arXiv 2404.16349, SODA 2025). These algorithms are 'galactic': the constants are so huge that nobody uses them in practice, but each improvement sharpens our understanding of how fast linear algebra can fundamentally be.
items.headline: New bounds reduce the theoretical cost of matrix multiplication

items.title: The asymptotics of r(4,t)
items.authors: Sam Mattheus, Jacques Verstraete
items.summary: The off-diagonal Ramsey number r(4,t) is the smallest group of people that must contain either 4 mutual acquaintances or t mutual strangers. Erdős conjectured decades ago that it grows like t^3 up to logarithmic factors, and offered a cash prize. Mattheus and Verstraete proved a lower bound of order t^3/(log t)^4, matching the known upper bound up to a log factor. Their surprising method combined ideas from finite geometry (a structure called the Hermitian unital) with probabilistic arguments.
items.headline: New estimates sharpen a problem about unavoidable patterns in graphs

items.title: An aperiodic monotile
items.authors: David Smith, Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig S. Kaplan, Chaim Goodman-Strauss
items.summary: An aperiodic monotile, or 'einstein' (German for 'one stone'), is a single shape that can cover the whole plane with no gaps or overlaps but can never do so in a repeating pattern. Whether such a shape exists was an open problem for about 60 years. The 13-sided 'hat', found by hobbyist David Smith and proved aperiodic by the team with a mix of geometric argument and computer-assisted checking, is the first one ever discovered, and the paper actually gives a whole continuous family of such shapes.
items.headline: One shape can tile a plane without a repeating pattern

items.title: An exponential improvement for diagonal Ramsey
items.authors: Marcelo Campos, Simon Griffiths, Robert Morris, Julian Sahasrabudhe
items.summary: The Ramsey number R(k) is the smallest party size that guarantees either k mutual acquaintances or k mutual strangers. Since 1935 the best upper bound had been essentially 4^k, and improving the base 4 was one of the most famous open problems in combinatorics. Campos, Griffiths, Morris and Sahasrabudhe proved R(k) is at most (4 - epsilon)^k for a small fixed epsilon, the first exponential improvement in nearly 90 years. The proof introduces a new 'book algorithm' for building large monochromatic structures.
items.headline: A new bound advances a classic Ramsey-theory problem

items.title: Strong Bounds for 3-Progressions
items.authors: Zander Kelley, Raghu Meka
items.summary: A 3-term arithmetic progression is three numbers evenly spaced, like 4, 9, 14. Kelley and Meka proved that any set of whole numbers up to N that avoids all such triples must be tiny: its size shrinks like N divided by an exponential of a power of log N, far smaller than the previous best bound of roughly N/(log N). This settles a question going back to Erdős and Turán in 1936 in a form close to what Behrend's 1946 construction shows is possible, and the new analytic techniques have already been reused across additive combinatorics.
items.headline: A stronger bound limits sets without three-term arithmetic progressions

items.title: Completion of the Liquid Tensor Experiment
items.authors: Johan Commelin (lead), Adam Topaz, Peter Scholze and the Lean mathlib community
items.summary: In December 2020 Fields medallist Peter Scholze challenged the Lean community to formally verify a key theorem from his and Dustin Clausen's 'condensed mathematics', a new foundation for doing analysis with algebraic tools, because he was not fully confident in his own proof. Formal verification means rewriting every step in the Lean proof assistant so a computer checks the logic with no gaps. Led by Johan Commelin, the project finished on 14 July 2022, about 18 months after the challenge, and confirmed the theorem. It was the first time cutting-edge research mathematics had been machine-checked in this way, and it forced a large expansion of mathlib, Lean's shared library of formalised mathematics.
items.headline: A proof assistant verifies a difficult result in modern analysis

items.title: Fields Medals 2022: Duminil-Copin, Huh, Maynard, Viazovska
items.authors: International Mathematical Union
items.summary: The Fields Medal is awarded every four years to up to four mathematicians under 40 and is often compared to a Nobel Prize. The 2022 medals went to Hugo Duminil-Copin (phase transitions in statistical physics, such as when a material suddenly becomes magnetic), June Huh (bringing tools from algebraic geometry into combinatorics), James Maynard (the structure of prime numbers, including small gaps between primes) and Maryna Viazovska (proving that the E8 lattice is the densest way to pack identical spheres in 8 dimensions). Viazovska is only the second woman to receive the medal.
items.headline: The 2022 Fields Medals honor probability, geometry, number theory, and packing

items.title: Hugo Duminil-Copin receives the 2022 Fields Medal for probabilistic phase transitions
items.authors: Hugo Duminil-Copin (medalist); International Mathematical Union
items.venue: Fields Medals 2022, International Mathematical Union, awarded at the IMU Award Ceremony, Helsinki
items.summary: The Fields Medal, given every four years to mathematicians under 40, went to Hugo Duminil-Copin "for solving longstanding problems in the probabilistic theory of phase transitions in statistical physics, especially in dimensions three and four." A phase transition is a sudden change in behaviour when a parameter crosses a critical value, like water freezing; in percolation models you randomly keep or delete links in a grid and ask when a connected path across the whole grid appears. Duminil-Copin proved sharp, rigorous statements about where and how these transitions happen in models such as the Ising model of magnetism, turning physicists' long-standing conjectures into theorems.
items.headline: A Fields Medal recognizes mathematical work on phase transitions

items.title: Deep learning: a statistical viewpoint
items.authors: Peter L. Bartlett, Andrea Montanari, Alexander Rakhlin
items.summary: Classical statistics warns that a model with more adjustable parameters than data points will "overfit": memorise the training examples and predict poorly on new ones. Yet modern neural networks have billions of parameters, fit their training data perfectly, and still generalise well. This survey lays out the emerging mathematical explanation in three parts: overparametrisation makes it easy for simple gradient methods to find solutions that fit the data exactly; those methods implicitly prefer the "simplest" (minimum-norm) such solution; and in high dimensions this can produce "benign overfitting," where fitting noise exactly barely hurts predictions. The authors prove these effects rigorously for linear models and two-layer networks and lay out what remains open for realistic deep networks.
items.headline: Statistical theory examines why deep learning works

items.title: A meta-analysis of the relation between math anxiety and math achievement
items.authors: Connie Barroso, Colleen M. Ganley, Amanda L. McGraw, Elyssa A. Geer, Sara A. Hart, Mia C. Daucourt
items.summary: A meta-analysis pools the results of many separate studies to estimate an overall effect. This one combined hundreds of samples covering learners from primary school to adulthood and found a consistent, small-to-moderate negative correlation (around -0.3) between math anxiety, the fear or tension people feel when facing numbers, and actual math performance. The relationship held across grade levels and countries, though its strength varied with how anxiety and achievement were measured. It matters because it confirms that anxiety is not merely a symptom of being weak at math: it is an independent factor that educators can target, for example with low-stakes practice and reframing mistakes as part of learning.
items.headline: A meta-analysis examines the relationship between mathematics anxiety and achievement

items.title: Recombination: A Family of Markov Chains for Redistricting
items.authors: Daryl DeFord, Moon Duchin, Justin Solomon
items.summary: Gerrymandering is drawing electoral district boundaries to favour one party. To judge whether a map is an outlier, mathematicians generate an "ensemble" of thousands of alternative legal maps and compare the proposed map's partisan outcome against that distribution. This paper introduces ReCom (recombination), a Markov chain, a random-walk procedure, that repeatedly merges two neighbouring districts and re-splits them using a random spanning tree, producing compact, realistic districts far faster than earlier methods that moved one precinct at a time. The method underpins the open-source GerryChain software and has been used in expert testimony in U.S. redistricting court cases.
items.headline: Random sampling provides a reference for evaluating electoral maps

items.title: Randomized numerical linear algebra: Foundations and algorithms
items.authors: Per-Gunnar Martinsson, Joel A. Tropp
items.summary: Much of scientific computing and machine learning boils down to linear algebra on enormous matrices: solving systems of equations, finding a matrix's most important directions (low-rank approximation), or least-squares fitting. Randomized numerical linear algebra speeds these up by multiplying the matrix by a small random matrix (a "sketch") that preserves its essential geometry, then working with the much smaller result. This 170-page survey is the standard reference: it proves why sketching works, using concentration-of-measure ideas from probability, and gives practical algorithms for norm estimation, randomized SVD, streaming (single-pass) approximation, and kernel matrices that now ship in mainstream numerical libraries.
items.headline: Randomness speeds up calculations with large matrices

items.title: Induced subgraphs of hypercubes and a proof of the Sensitivity Conjecture
items.authors: Hao Huang
items.summary: A Boolean function takes a string of bits and outputs one bit. Its 'sensitivity' is the number of single input bits whose flipping changes the output, and since 1992 theoretical computer scientists had conjectured that sensitivity is polynomially related to other standard measures of a function's complexity (such as its degree as a polynomial). Huang proved it in a two-page argument: any set containing more than half the corners of an n-dimensional cube must contain a corner with at least the square root of n neighbours in the set, which he showed using a cleverly signed matrix. The proof was so short that it was verified worldwide within days and is now taught in courses, and it settled a nearly 30-year-old open problem in the theory of computation.
items.headline: A short proof resolves the sensitivity conjecture

items.title: Moving to a World Beyond "p < 0.05"
items.authors: Ronald L. Wasserstein, Allen L. Schirm, Nicole A. Lazar
items.venue: The American Statistician, vol. 73, sup1, pp. 1-19 (editorial for the special issue "Statistical Inference in the 21st Century")
items.summary: A p-value measures how surprising your data would be if there were truly no effect; for decades a result with p below 0.05 has been labelled "statistically significant" and treated as a discovery. Building on the American Statistical Association's 2016 statement on p-values, this editorial introducing a 43-paper special issue argues that researchers should stop using the phrase "statistically significant" altogether, because a single cutoff turns a continuous measure of evidence into a misleading yes/no verdict. It recommends reporting uncertainty honestly, thinking about effect sizes and context, and treating p-values as one input among many rather than a gatekeeper for publication.
items.headline: Statisticians argue against treating p = 0.05 as a magic boundary

items.title: Many Analysts, One Data Set: Making Transparent How Variations in Analytic Choices Affect Results
items.authors: Raphael Silberzahn, Eric L. Uhlmann, Daniel P. Martin, and 58 co-authors
items.venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, vol. 1, no. 3, pp. 337-356
items.summary: Twenty-nine research teams (61 analysts) were given the identical dataset and the identical question: are soccer referees more likely to give red cards to darker-skinned players? Twenty teams (69%) found a statistically significant effect and nine (31%) did not, with estimated effect sizes ranging from 0.89 to 2.93 in odds-ratio units, and the teams used 21 different combinations of control variables. Neither expertise nor prior beliefs explained the spread. The study is a landmark of the replication-crisis literature because it shows that honest, competent analysts can reach different conclusions from the same data simply through defensible analytic choices, which is why pre-registration and multiverse analyses are now recommended.
items.headline: Different analysts reach different results from the same data

items.title: A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture (the Flyspeck project)
items.authors: Thomas Hales, Mark Adams, Gertrud Bauer, Tat Dat Dang, John Harrison, et al. (22 authors)
items.venue: Forum of Mathematics, Pi, vol. 5, e2
items.summary: Background entry. Kepler's 1611 conjecture says no way of stacking identical spheres is denser than the familiar grocery-store pyramid. Thomas Hales proved it in 1998, but the proof relied on hundreds of pages and large computer calculations, and the referees for Annals of Mathematics said they could only be '99% certain' it was correct. Hales then launched Flyspeck, an 11-year project completed in August 2014 that rewrote the whole proof in the HOL Light and Isabelle proof assistants so that a computer verified every logical step; the write-up was published in 2017. It was the largest formal proof of its time and a major reason mathematicians began to take machine-checked proofs seriously.
items.headline: A computer-checked proof settles the densest packing of equal spheres

items.title: The Millennium Prize Problems
items.authors: Clay Mathematics Institute
items.summary: Reference entry. On 24 May 2000 in Paris the Clay Mathematics Institute named seven problems and offered one million US dollars for the solution of each: the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, the Hodge conjecture, existence and smoothness for the Navier-Stokes equations, P versus NP, the Riemann hypothesis, Yang-Mills existence and mass gap, and the Poincaré conjecture. Only the Poincaré conjecture has been solved, by Grigori Perelman in 2002-2003; he declined the prize. P versus NP asks whether every problem whose answer can be quickly checked can also be quickly solved, and is the one most directly about computers. Claims of solutions appear regularly online and in preprints; none of the six remaining problems is accepted as solved as of September 2026.
items.headline: The Millennium Prize Problems define seven major mathematical challenges
